problem: Prior interactive visual navigation (RL agents that push away movable obstacles) chases success rate while ignoring the cost of interacting with the environment, and interactions can be counterproductive, e.g. pushing an obstacle so it blocks the existing path.
motivation: Unnecessary or harmful interactions are wasteful and risky in real settings, so an agent should weigh how an action will change the environment and the navigation task before acting. The paper argues that predicting local accessibility and penalizing interactions can yield more efficient navigation.
key_idea: Add a Local Accessibility Prediction (LAP) module so the agent anticipates how its next action affects the environment and navigability, and train it with a size-dependent interaction penalty in a two-stage pipeline.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations are visible. The claimed insight is that predicting the consequences of an action on local accessibility, combined with an explicit interaction cost that grows with obstacle size, reduces needless or counterproductive pushes while improving navigation performance.
method: Local Accessibility Prediction (LAP) module: lets the agent predict how the upcoming action will affect the environment and the navigation task before it decides.
Interaction penalty: a reward term representing the cost of interacting with the environment, with a different penalty depending on the size of the obstacle pushed away.
New metric: the average number of interactions is introduced as an evaluation metric.
Two-stage training pipeline: used to reach better learning performance (details not given in the abstract).
